stories.title: Clio Launches Vincent AI Mobile App, Extends Legal AI to Smartphones
stories.research_brief:
<cite index="4-2,4-3,4-4,4-5">Clio, a leader in legal AI, today announced the launch of the Vincent by Clio mobile app, extending Vincent's legal AI capabilities to iOS and Android OS for the first time. Vincent has become a core tool for lawyers analyzing legal issues, reviewing documents, and developing legal arguments. With the launch of the Vincent by Clio mobile App, those capabilities are no longer limited to the desktop. Lawyers can now ask questions, analyze documents, and get grounded answers backed by authority directly from their phones, allowing legal work to begin the moment a question or document surfaces.</cite>

<cite index="4-6,4-7,4-8">For Clio Work users, the Vincent by Clio mobile app can also draw on the full context of a matter, including client communications, deadlines, and case activity, so analysis reflects what's actually happening in the case. Lawyers can ask questions, review new developments, and explore strategy with that context already in place, helping ensure continuity across their work. This connection allows legal teams to move seamlessly between case management and legal analysis, making it easier to respond to new filings, prepare for what's next, and keep work moving from anywhere.</cite>

The mobile launch represents Clio's strategic expansion of its AI capabilities beyond traditional desktop environments. As one of the watch list companies in the legal AI space, Clio continues to build on its legal practice management foundation by adding AI-powered legal analysis tools. The mobile app allows lawyers to access AI assistance while on-the-go, potentially changing how legal work is conducted outside the office.

This launch comes as legal AI adoption accelerates across firms of all sizes. The integration with Clio's existing practice management platform provides context that standalone AI tools cannot offer, potentially giving Clio a competitive advantage in the increasingly crowded legal AI market.

stories.title: Manhattan Court Rules AI Chats Not Protected by Attorney-Client Privilege
stories.research_brief:
<cite index="21-1,21-2">In the case of United States v. Heppner, U.S. District Judge Jed S. Rakoff ordered a defendant to hand over 31 documents created with Anthropic's Claude AI chatbot, ruling that the AI-generated materials were not protected by privilege. The court found the exchanges failed to meet basic privilege requirements, as they were not communications with a lawyer, the user could not reasonably expect confidentiality, and the work was not performed at the direction of counsel.</cite> <cite index="21-3">On February 17, 2026, Judge Rakoff issued a written opinion on the case.</cite>

<cite index="21-4,21-10,21-11,21-12">In the wake of the ruling, law firms began revising engagement letters and circulating AI warnings to clients. A recent Manhattan federal court ruling has prompted major law firms to warn clients that anything shared with consumer AI chatbots can be subject to legal discovery, leading lawyers to recommend using only enterprise-level AI tools with contractual confidentiality guarantees when handling sensitive information. This ruling highlights the legal risks of using consumer-facing AI chatbots for anything related to active or potential litigation, as courts may not recognize attorney-client privilege or work product protections for content shared with these public platforms. Law firms are now scrambling to revise client contracts and internal policies to mitigate these new legal liabilities.</cite>

<cite index="8-12,8-13,8-14">Some firms said AI legal research is more likely to be protected by attorney-client privilege when it is conducted at the direction of a lawyer. If a lawyer does advise the use of AI, a person should say so in the chatbot prompt, New York-headquartered law firm Debevoise & Plimpton said in a notice on its website. "I am doing this research at the direction of counsel for X litigation," the firm suggested people write.</cite>

This ruling has significant implications for how lawyers and clients can safely use AI tools. The case involved Bradley Heppner, former chair of bankrupt financial services company GWG Holdings, who used Claude to prepare reports about his case. The court's decision establishes that simply using AI for legal work does not automatically create privilege protection, potentially exposing sensitive information in litigation.

stories.title: State AI Bill Wave: Nebraska, Maryland, Maine Pass New Chatbot and AI Laws
stories.research_brief:
<cite index="24-8,24-14,24-15,24-16,24-17">Legislatures in Nebraska (chatbot bill), Maryland (pricing), and Maine (health) passed AI bills last week. Legislatures in three states passed bills last week. Nebraska's unicameral legislature passed a chatbot bill. Maryland's legislature passed a pricing bill. Maine's legislature passed a bill that prohibits any person from providing, advertising or otherwise offering therapy or psychotherapy services, including through the use of AI, to the public unless the services are provided by</cite> licensed professionals.

<cite index="24-2,24-3,24-4,24-5,24-6,24-7">Nebraska's unicameral legislature passed LB 525. The first portion of the bill is the Agricultural Data Privacy Act while the second portion of the bill is the Conversational AI Safety Act. The chatbot portion of the bill regulates minors' interaction with conversational AI services, including requiring the service to disclose to minors that it is AI. The bill also requires operators of conversational AI services to disclose to persons that the service is not human if a reasonable person would not understand the service is not human. Among other things, the service also cannot represent or state that it is designed to provide professional mental or behavioral health care. If signed into law, the bill would be enforceable by the state attorney general.</cite>

This represents part of a broader state-level regulatory push on AI. <cite index="25-3,25-4">Since we last posted in mid-March, we have gone from 6 new AI laws passed in 2026 to 25! Another 27 bills have passed both chambers in their legislative process and could be on their way to becoming law soon.</cite> The focus appears to be on chatbot safety, particularly protections for minors, and restrictions on AI in healthcare settings.

<cite index="29-1,29-7">AI companions and chatbot safety continued to be a focus of state lawmakers this quarter, with new laws enacted in Washington (HB 2225), Oregon (SB 1546), and Idaho (Conversational AI Safety Act (SB 1297)).</cite> This trend reflects growing concerns about AI chatbots' interactions with vulnerable populations, especially children, and their potential misuse in professional services like therapy.
